course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 2. In Module 1, you learned why selling milk daily can change your life. Now we get to the heart of the business: the dairy herd formula. This formula is simple: your daily milk sales depend on three numbers: how many cows you milk, how much milk each cow gives, and how many days you sell. But the real magic is in the fourth number: your cost per litre. If you know these numbers, you can predict your profit and fix problems before they eat your money. In Africa, many small dairy farmers fail because they guess. They guess how much milk they get, guess how much feed costs, and guess why some cows give less. Guessing leads to losses. The dairy herd formula replaces guessing with counting. For example, if you have 5 cows giving 8 litres each, that's 40 litres a day. If you sell at 50 KES per litre, that's 2,000 KES daily. But if your feed, labour, and health costs are 1,500 KES, your profit is only 500 KES. Now imagine you improve feed and each cow gives 12 litres. You now have 60 litres, earning 3,000 KES, and profit jumps to 1,500 KES. That's the power of the formula. It also helps you decide when to cull a cow, when to buy feed in bulk, and when to hire help. This module will teach you the tools, the step-by-step method, common mistakes, safety, and give you a practical exercise. By the end, you will be able to calculate your own herd's daily milk sales and profit with confidence. Remember: what gets measured gets managed. Let's start measuring.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To use the dairy herd formula, you don't need expensive equipment. You need a few simple tools that cost little but save you big money. First, a record book. Any exercise book will do, but a hardcover one lasts longer. You will record daily milk yield per cow, feed given, and any health issues. Second, a measuring jug or a calibrated bucket. You must measure milk accurately, not by eye. A 10-litre plastic bucket with litre markings is perfect. Third, a weighing scale for feed. A simple hanging scale or a bathroom scale works. You need to know exactly how much feed each cow gets. Fourth, a chalkboard or whiteboard for your shed. Write today's milk total and feed cost so everyone sees it. Fifth, a mobile phone. Use it for a calculator, a calendar, and to take photos of records. You can also use free apps like 'Milk Manager' or 'Farm Records' if you have internet. Sixth, a notebook for individual cow cards. Each cow gets a page: her name or number, calving date, daily milk, and breeding dates. Seventh, a simple first aid kit for udder care: clean cloths, iodine, and teat dip. Eighth, a feed storage container with a lid to keep feed dry and safe from rats. Ninth, a water bucket or trough with measurements so you know water intake. Tenth, a pen and permanent marker to label cow cards. All these tools together cost less than 2,000 KES if you buy locally. In Africa, you can find them at agrovet shops or markets. The most important tool is discipline: use them every day, at the same time. Without records, the formula is just numbers on paper. With records, it becomes your roadmap to profit.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps every day to apply the dairy herd formula. Step 1: Identify each cow. Give every milking cow a number or name. Write it on a card. Step 2: Measure milk per cow. At each milking (morning and evening), use your calibrated bucket. Record the litres for each cow separately. If you milk twice, add both. Step 3: Total daily milk. Add all cows' litres. Example: Cow 1 gives 10L, Cow 2 gives 8L, Cow 3 gives 12L. Total = 30 litres. Step 4: Calculate average per cow. Divide total by number of cows. 30 Ã· 3 = 10 litres per cow. Step 5: Record feed. Weigh the feed you give each cow. If you feed concentrates, note the kilograms. Also note forage (hay, silage, grass) in bundles or kg. Step 6: Calculate feed cost. Multiply kg of feed by price per kg. Example: 2 kg concentrate at 40 KES/kg = 80 KES per cow. For 3 cows, 240 KES. Step 7: Add other daily costs. Labour, water, electricity, and health care. Divide monthly costs by 30 to get daily. Example: labour 300 KES/day, water 50 KES/day, health 20 KES/day. Total other = 370 KES. Step 8: Total daily cost. Feed cost + other costs. 240 + 370 = 610 KES. Step 9: Calculate revenue. Total milk litres Ã selling price. 30L Ã 50 KES = 1,500 KES. Step 10: Calculate profit. Revenue â total cost. 1,500 â 610 = 890 KES profit per day. Step 11: Calculate cost per litre. Total cost Ã· total litres. 610 Ã· 30 = 20.33 KES per litre. Step 12: Compare to selling price. If selling price is 50 KES, your margin is 29.67 KES per litre. Step 13: Set targets. If you want 1,200 KES profit daily, you need to either increase litres or reduce cost per litre. Step 14: Review weekly. Look for cows giving less than average. Check feed quality. Step 15: Adjust. If a cow gives 5L but eats 2kg feed, she may be losing money. Consider culling or treating. Repeat daily. This method turns your herd into a business you control.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Not measuring milk per cow. Many farmers just look at the total bucket. Fix: Use individual cow records. You cannot manage what you don't measure. Mistake 2: Guessing feed amounts. If you feed by handfuls, you overfeed some and underfeed others. Fix: Weigh feed with a scale. Use a standard measure like a 2kg tin. Mistake 3: Ignoring cost per litre. You might sell milk at 50 KES but spend 45 KES to produce it. Fix: Calculate cost per litre weekly. If it's above 70% of selling price, find savings. Mistake 4: Feeding low-quality forage. In dry season, poor grass gives less milk. Fix: Invest in hay or silage. One bale of hay can add 2 litres per cow per day. Mistake 5: Not culling unproductive cows. A cow that gives 3 litres but eats like a 15-litre cow is a parasite. Fix: Use the formula: if a cow's daily feed cost exceeds her milk value for 3 months, sell her. Mistake 6: Water shortage. Cows need 60-100 litres of water daily. If water is limited, milk drops. Fix: Provide clean water always. A cow giving 20 litres needs 80 litres of water. Mistake 7: Poor record keeping. Records on loose papers get lost. Fix: Use a single notebook or a phone app. Back up with photos. Mistake 8: Selling milk on credit. You lose cash flow and can't buy feed. Fix: Sell for cash or mobile money. If you must give credit, limit to trusted customers and keep a ledger. Mistake 9: Ignoring cow health. Mastitis, ticks, and worms reduce milk. Fix: Dip cows weekly, deworm every 3 months, and check udders daily. Mistake 10: Overstocking. Too many cows on small land leads to feed shortage. Fix: Keep only as many cows as your land and budget can feed well. Each mistake has a fix. Start with the biggest one in your herd today.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety in dairy farming protects you, your workers, and your cows. First, personal safety. Always wear clean overalls and gumboots when handling cows. Cows can kick, especially during milking. Never stand directly behind a cow. Use a kick bar or tie her legs gently if she is nervous. Wash your hands with soap before and after milking. Second, milk safety. Clean the udder with a clean cloth and warm water before milking. Use a separate cloth for each cow to prevent mastitis spread. After milking, dip teats in iodine solution. Filter milk immediately using a clean cloth or filter. Cool milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours if you sell to a processor. If you sell raw, keep it in a clean container and sell within 4 hours. Third, feed safety. Never feed mouldy hay or silage. Mould causes aflatoxin, which passes into milk and harms people. Store feed on pallets, off the floor, in a dry place. Keep rats out. Fourth, chemical safety. Store veterinary drugs, pesticides, and dips away from feed and milk. Use gloves when handling. Follow withdrawal periods: do not sell milk from a cow treated with antibiotics for at least 3 days after last dose. Fifth, animal welfare. Provide shade, clean bedding, and space. Cows that are stressed give less milk. Handle them calmly. Sixth, record safety. Keep records in a safe, dry place. Take photos as backup. Seventh, financial safety. Keep business money separate from household money. Pay yourself a salary. Save 10% of profit for emergencies. Eighth, best practice: milk at the same times daily, 12 hours apart. Keep a regular routine. Train your workers on these practices. Post a simple checklist on the shed wall. Review safety monthly. A safe farm is a profitable farm.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice the dairy herd formula with your own herd or a sample herd. If you don't have cows yet, use the example below. Follow these steps and write your answers in your record book. Step 1: Choose 3 cows. If you have cows, pick three. If not, use: Cow A gives 12L, Cow B gives 8L, Cow C gives 5L daily. Step 2: Calculate total daily milk. 12+8+5 = 25 litres. Step 3: Calculate average per cow. 25 Ã· 3 = 8.33 litres. Step 4: Record feed per cow. Assume each cow gets 2kg of dairy meal at 45 KES/kg, and 10kg of forage at 5 KES/kg. Feed cost per cow = (2Ã45) + (10Ã5) = 90 + 50 = 140 KES. For 3 cows, total feed = 420 KES. Step 5: Add other daily costs. Labour 200 KES, water 30 KES, health 20 KES, transport 50 KES. Total other = 300 KES. Step 6: Total daily cost = 420 + 300 = 720 KES. Step 7: Calculate revenue. Sell at 55 KES/litre. 25L Ã 55 = 1,375 KES. Step 8: Calculate profit = 1,375 â 720 = 655 KES. Step 9: Calculate cost per litre = 720 Ã· 25 = 28.8 KES. Step 10: Margin per litre = 55 â 28.8 = 26.2 KES. Step 11: Identify the least productive cow. Cow C gives 5L. Her feed cost is 140 KES. Her milk value = 5Ã55 = 275 KES. She still makes a profit of 135 KES, but less than others. Step 12: What if you improve feed for Cow C to 3kg dairy meal? Feed cost becomes (3Ã45)+50 = 185 KES. If milk increases to 8L, revenue = 440 KES, profit = 255 KES. Better. Step 13: Set a target. If you want 1,000 KES profit daily, how many litres at 55 KES with cost per litre 28.8? Profit per litre = 26.2. Need 1000 Ã· 26.2 = 38.2 litres. You need 13 more litres. Step 14: Write your action plan. Example: add 1kg feed to Cow C, check water, and cull if no improvement in 30 days. Step 15: Repeat this exercise weekly with real numbers. Bring your results to the next session.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: The Dairy Herd Formula

This practical reference sheet is the working companion to the Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System course. It pulls together the numbers, tables, tools and habits that turn a herd of cows into a predictable daily milk business. Use it at the farm gate, in the milk shed, and when you review your week's sales. The goal is simple: know how many litres you can sell tomorrow, and know what it costs you to produce them.

In most African dairy systems â from Kiambu and Nakuru in Kenya to Wakiso in Uganda, Bahati in Tanzania, and the smallholder clusters around Harare and Lusaka â the difference between a profitable dairy enterprise and a break-even one is not the breed of cow alone. It is the system: consistent feeding, clean water, controlled breeding, reliable record-keeping, and honest cost accounting. The Dairy Herd Formula gives you a single framework to manage all of these.

Table 1: Typical daily milk yield benchmarks by production system

Production system Typical yield (L/cow/day) Lactation length (days) Common African context
Indigenous / Zebu (e.g. Boran, N'Dama) 1.5 â 3.0 180 â 240 Pastoral and agropastoral systems, Sahel and Horn of Africa
Improved crossbreed (F1âF3) 6.0 â 12.0 270 â 305 Smallholder zero-grazing, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania
Exotic purebred (Friesian, Ayrshire, Jersey) 12.0 â 25.0 305 â 330 Commercial and peri-urban dairy farms
Well-managed crossbreed (top quartile) 15.0 â 20.0 305 â 320 Intensive zero-grazing with balanced rations

Source: FAO, Dairy Development in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Review of Issues and Options (2011); and ILRI, Smallholder Dairy Production and Marketing (East Africa working papers). Yields vary widely with feeding, genetics and management.

Table 2: Cost and margin example â 10 milking cows, 15 L/cow/day

Milking cowsn10
Yield per cowL15 L
Total daily milkn Ã L150 L
Less home use (5%)150 Ã 0.057.5 L

Gross income130.5 Ã 0.4558.73

Estimated daily margin58.73 â 44.0514.68

Source: Cost structure adapted from ILRI/FAO smallholder dairy budget analyses (East Africa) and Kenya Dairy Board farm-gate price monitoring. Figures are illustrative â replace with your own farm records.

â  SAFETY WARNING â MILK HANDLING AND ANIMAL HEALTH

  • Never sell milk from a cow treated with antibiotics until the full withdrawal period stated on the drug label has passed. Residues harm consumers and can shut you out of formal markets.
  • Cool milk to below 4 Â°C within 2 hours of milking, or deliver to the collection point immediately. Warm milk is a bacterial breeding ground and spoils within hours in tropical heat.
  • Wash hands and udders with clean water before milking. Use a separate clean cloth per cow where possible to avoid spreading mastitis.
  • Do not use untreated river water to dilute or rinse milk. Always use potable water â contamination is the fastest route to rejected deliveries.
  • Store and handle pesticides, acaricides and veterinary drugs away from the milk room. Never decant chemicals into milk or feed containers.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Count and record the number of cows actually in milk today â not the total herd.
  • â Record the morning and evening yield per cow, or at least the herd total.
  • â Subtract home use and calf milk before calculating saleable litres.
  • â Confirm your farm-gate or cooperative price per litre for the current week.
  • â Track feed cost per litre â if it exceeds 60% of the milk price, review the ration.
  • â Check water availability: a milking cow needs 60â100 litres of clean water per day.
  • â Verify withdrawal periods for any animal under treatment before the milk goes to market.
  • â Update the daily margin (income minus feed, labour and health costs) at least weekly.
  • â Review lactation days and plan breeding so calving is spread to keep milk flowing year-round.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Dairy Production and Products: global dairy data, guidelines and country profiles.
  • FAO â Dairy Development in Sub-Saharan Africa: free full-text review of smallholder dairy systems.
  • ILRI â Livestock Genetics and Dairy Research: breeding, crossbreeding and productivity studies for Africa.
  • Kenya Dairy Board â Regulations, milk quality and market information: useful for East African producers.
  • CGIAR / ILRI â CGSpace repository: search "smallholder dairy" for free technical and economic reports.

Practical tip: The Dairy Herd Formula only works if the numbers going in are honest. A cow that gives 12 litres on paper but 8 in the bucket will quietly destroy your margin. Weigh or measure milk daily, write it down, and let the formula tell you the truth â then fix the weakest input first.

quiz.q: What is the dairy herd formula mainly used for?
options: A) To calculate daily milk sales and profit
quiz.explanation: The formula helps you calculate daily milk sales and profit based on milk yield, costs, and selling price.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a tool needed for the dairy herd formula?
quiz.explanation: A tractor is not essential for daily milk sales record keeping; simple tools like a record book, jug, and scale are enough.

quiz.q: Why is it important to measure milk per cow?
options: A) To know which cow is profitable
B) To make the milk taste better
quiz.explanation: Measuring per cow helps identify high and low producers so you can manage feed and culling decisions.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the step-by-step method?
quiz.explanation: You must identify each cow (by number or name) before you can record her milk yield.

quiz.q: If you have 4 cows giving 10L, 8L, 12L, and 6L, what is the total daily milk?
How do you calculate average milk per cow?
options: A) Total milk Ã number of cows
B) Total milk Ã· number of cows
C) Total milk + number of cows
D) Total milk â number of cows
quiz.explanation: Average per cow is total daily milk divided by the number of milking cows.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when feeding cows?
quiz.explanation: Guessing feed amounts leads to overfeeding or underfeeding, which wastes money and reduces milk.

quiz.q: What does cost per litre tell you?
options: A) How much you spend to produce one litre of milk
B) How much milk a cow gives
C) How many cows you have
D) How much water a cow drinks
quiz.explanation: Cost per litre is total daily cost divided by total litres produced, showing your production efficiency.

quiz.q: If total daily cost is 800 KES and you produce 40 litres, what is cost per litre?
quiz.explanation: 800 Ã· 40 = 20 KES per litre.

quiz.q: Why should you cull an unproductive cow?
options: A) She eats feed but gives little milk
D) She is a different breed
quiz.explanation: An unproductive cow costs more in feed than she returns in milk value, reducing overall profit.

quiz.q: What is a safe practice after milking?
options: D) Sell milk immediately without cooling
quiz.explanation: Teat dipping prevents mastitis and keeps the cow healthy for future milk production.

quiz.q: How much water does a cow giving 20 litres of milk need daily?
quiz.explanation: A cow needs about 4 litres of water for every litre of milk, so 20L milk requires roughly 80L water.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in record keeping?
options: B) Keeping records on loose papers
quiz.explanation: Loose papers get lost easily; a single notebook or phone app is more reliable.

quiz.q: What should you do if a cow is treated with antibiotics?
options: B) Discard milk for at least 3 days
C) Mix her milk with others
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics can pass into milk; you must observe the withdrawal period (usually 3 days) before selling.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, what is the total daily cost for 3 cows?
quiz.explanation: Feed cost 420 KES plus other costs 300 KES equals 720 KES total daily cost.

quiz.q: What is the profit if revenue is 1,375 KES and total cost is 720 KES?
quiz.explanation: 1,375 â 720 = 655 KES profit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep business money separate from household money?
options: A) To avoid mixing expenses and know true profit
quiz.explanation: Separating money helps you track business performance and avoid spending profit on household needs.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for feed storage?
options: B) Store on pallets in dry place
quiz.explanation: Storing feed on pallets in a dry place prevents mould and contamination.

quiz.q: How often should you review your dairy herd formula records?
quiz.explanation: Weekly review helps you spot trends and make timely adjustments, though daily recording is also done.

quiz.q: What is the margin per litre if selling price is 55 KES and cost per litre is 28.8 KES?
quiz.explanation: 55 â 28.8 = 26.2 KES margin per litre.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety risk when handling cows?
quiz.explanation: Standing directly behind a cow puts you at risk of being kicked.

quiz.q: What should you do with milk from a cow with mastitis?
quiz.explanation: Milk from a mastitis cow contains bacteria and antibiotics; it must be discarded.

quiz.q: What is the target profit in the practical exercise if you want 1,000 KES daily?
quiz.explanation: Profit per litre is 26.2 KES, so 1000 Ã· 26.2 â 38.2 litres needed.

quiz.q: Why is clean water important for dairy cows?
options: B) It makes milk taste better
quiz.explanation: Water is essential for milk production; shortage reduces yield significantly.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when selling milk?
options: B) Selling on credit without records
quiz.explanation: Selling on credit without a ledger leads to lost income and cash flow problems.

quiz.q: What should you do before milking?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the udder with warm water and a clean cloth prevents dirt and bacteria from entering milk.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a chalkboard in the shed?
options: A) It shows daily milk total and feed cost
quiz.explanation: A chalkboard makes key numbers visible to all workers, improving accountability.

quiz.q: How can you improve milk yield from a low-producing cow?
options: A) Increase feed quality and quantity
quiz.explanation: Better feed (especially energy and protein) often increases milk yield before culling.

quiz.q: What is a withdrawal period?
options: A) Time after drug treatment before selling milk
C) Time to train a cow
quiz.explanation: Withdrawal period is the waiting time after medication to ensure drug residues are out of milk.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the dairy herd formula?
options: A) To make daily milk sales profitable
quiz.explanation: The formula helps you track and improve the profitability of your daily milk sales.
